title: Rounding
subtitle: Round whole numbers and decimals, one step at a time.

learn.title: What is rounding?
paragraphs: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby, simpler number. It helps us describe amounts without giving every digit.
To round to the nearest 10, choose the closest multiple of 10. For example, 67 is closer to 70 than to 60.
learn.note: The symbol ≈ means “approximately equal to”. Rounding gives an approximation, so the value can change.

learn.title: Which ten is nearest?
paragraphs: Move the number along the line. Watch which multiple of 10 is closest.
65 is halfway between 60 and 70. When a positive number is exactly halfway, we round up.

learn.title: Look one digit to the right
paragraphs: Find the place you are rounding to. Then look at the digit immediately to its right.
0, 1, 2, 3 or 4: keep the rounding digit the same. 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9: increase it by 1.
learn.note: Replace whole-number digits to the right with zeros. To the nearest 100, the deciding digit is 6, so 367 rounds to 400.

learn.title: Rounding decimal places
paragraphs: Decimal places count digits after the decimal point. One decimal place keeps tenths; two decimal places keep hundredths.
To round 4.276 to 2 decimal places, keep the hundredths digit, 7. The next digit is 6, so increase 7 to 8.
learn.note: Leave out decimal digits beyond the requested place. Keep trailing zeros when they show the requested accuracy: 3.04 to 1 decimal place is 3.0.

learn.title: Rounding significant figures
paragraphs: Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit, wherever it is in the number.
In 0.004782, the first significant figure is 4 and the second is 7. The next digit is 8, so 7 increases to 8.
learn.note: Starting zeros do not count. Zeros between non-zero digits do count: in 3,062, the first two significant figures are 3 and 0. To 2 significant figures, 3,062 rounds to 3,100.

learn.title: When rounding carries into the next column
paragraphs: Sometimes increasing a digit gives 10. Carry the 1 into the column to the left, just as you would when adding.
Round 9.96 to 1 decimal place. The hundredths digit is 6, so the tenths must increase. The carry changes 9.9 into 10.0.
learn.note: Always return to the original number when changing accuracy. For example, 2.449 rounds directly to 2.4 at 1 decimal place. Do not round to 2.45 first, then to 2.5.

guided.target_help: The tens digit is the place to keep.
guided.decider_help: The ones digit is immediately to its right.
guided.explanation: 7 is at least 5. Increase 6 tens to 7 tens and replace the ones with 0.

guided.target_help: The hundreds digit is the place to keep.
guided.decider_help: Look at the tens digit, immediately to the right.
guided.explanation: 4 is less than 5. Keep 6 hundreds and replace the tens and ones with zeros.

guided.target_help: Keep the digit in the thousands column.
guided.decider_help: The hundreds digit decides which thousand is nearest.
guided.explanation: 3 is less than 5. Keep 4 thousands and replace the other digits with zeros.

guided.target_help: Two decimal places means keeping the hundredths digit.
guided.decider_help: Look at the thousandths digit, one place to the right.
guided.explanation: 6 is at least 5. Increase the hundredths from 7 to 8, then leave out the thousandths.

guided.target_help: Start counting at the first non-zero digit, 4. The second significant figure is 7.
guided.decider_help: The next digit after the second significant figure decides whether to round up.
guided.explanation: 8 is at least 5. Increase 7 to 8. Keep the starting zeros: 0.0048.

guided.target_help: One decimal place means keeping the tenths digit.
guided.decider_help: Use the hundredths digit, immediately to the right of the tenths.
guided.explanation: 6 is at least 5. Increasing 9 tenths causes a carry into the ones, then the tens: 10.0.

practice.explanation: The ones digit is 3, so keep 8 tens and replace the ones with 0.
650 is halfway between 600 and 700. The tens digit is 5, so round up.
The hundreds digit is 3, so keep 4 thousands.
Keep the tenths digit, 7. The hundredths digit is 3, so it stays 7.
The thousandths digit is 6, so the hundredths digit increases from 5 to 6.
The hundredths digit is 4, so the tenths digit stays 0. Write 3.0 to show 1 decimal place.
Keep 7 and 4. The next digit is 6, so increase 4 to 5, then use zeros.
The first two significant figures are 6 and 3. The next digit is 8, so increase 3 to 4.
The hundredths digit is 7. Rounding up carries into the ones and tens: 10.0.

practice.prompt: A path is 248 metres long. Round its length to the nearest 10 metres.
practice.explanation: The ones digit is 8, so 248 is closer to 250 than to 240.

check.prompt: A stadium has 2,748 spectators. Round this to the nearest 100.
check.explanation: The tens digit is 4, so keep 7 hundreds: 2,700.
The deciding digit is 5, so the hundredths digit increases from 6 to 7.
Start counting at 7. Keep 7 and 2; the next digit is 6, so round up.

check.prompt: Amir says: “4.95 rounds to 4.9 at 1 decimal place.” Which explanation is correct?
check.answer: The 5 rounds the tenths up, giving 5.0.
check.explanation: The hundredths digit is 5. Increasing 9 tenths causes a carry, so the result is 5.0.
options: The 5 rounds the tenths up, giving 5.0.
Keep 4.9 because the tenths digit is already 9.
Round to 4 because only whole numbers can be rounded.

check.prompt: A bottle holds 1.049 litres. Round this directly to 1 decimal place.
check.explanation: The hundredths digit in the original number is 4, so the tenths stay 0. Write 1.0.
